question.text: A series <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi><mi>R</mi></math> circuit is connected to a voltage source with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi><mfenced separators="|"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>sin</mi><mfenced><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> . After a very large time, current <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>I</mi><mfenced separators="|"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></math> behaves as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced separators="|"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>≫</mo><mfrac><mi>L</mi><mi>R</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>:

solution.text:
When sinusoidal voltage is applied across LR circuit, current is also sinusoidal but it lags by some phase.

Current will be in the form of
I=I0sinωt-ϕ
Graph will be sinusoidal.

Here I0 is the maximum current and ϕ is phase difference between V & I
